name: tessera-live
producer: Trillian Tessera v1.0.4 (github.com/transparency-dev/tessera), its POSIX example cmd/examples/posix-oneshot built with go1.27.1 on a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runner; a C2SP tlog-tiles log -- entry bundles, hash tiles and an Ed25519-signed checkpoint (C2SP signed note). Tessera is the library Sigstore's Rekor v2 (sigstore/rekor-tiles) is built on; its go.mod on main requires tessera v1.0.4. This is not a Rekor deployment
description: A live capture, 2026-09-30, and the positive control for integrity: six audit statements appended in two rounds (3 + 3), with the signed checkpoint kept after each. Tessera's own client built an inclusion proof for every entry and a consistency proof from the size-3 checkpoint to the size-6 checkpoint, and all verified (verify.jsonl); examples/third-party/tessera-live/verify_tlog.py, standard library only, reaches the same result independently: signature, RFC 6962 root over the entries equal to the signed root, level-0 tile equal to the leaf hashes, every proof. Flipping one byte of one entry made that entry's inclusion proof fail (verify-tampered.jsonl). tessera-live-scrubbed.jsonl removes the refused delete_file entry: verify_tlog.py rejects it (size 6 signed, 5 entries, root mismatch, index gap). conformance.py up to 1.4.2-draft, which had no Merkle-tree mechanism (every mechanism was a hash chain), scored both files L0 and the scrubbed one exactly as the full one. From 1.4.3-draft (draft, EXT-026) the adapter declares merkle-tlog: the checker recomputes the RFC 6962 root over the delivered entries, compares it and the size with the checkpoint, and verifies the checkpoint's Ed25519 signature under log.vkey. The full file passes L1; the scrubbed file fails VLC-L1-1.
_basis: Captured, not read from documentation: workflow .github/workflows/falco-rekor-capture.yml, capture/scripts/tessera.sh and capture/scripts/tlogcap.go on branch capture/falco-rekor, run run-20260930T112902Z; the log directory, both checkpoints, the verifier key, the proof files and posix-oneshot's output are copied to examples/third-party/tessera-live/ (the log's .state/ directory was not uploaded by the capture job, which skips hidden files; it is Tessera's internal state, not part of the tlog-tiles read API). The signing key was generated on the runner and not kept. The version is from `go version -m` on the binary (posix-oneshot.buildinfo.txt). conformance.py MECHANISMS up to 1.4.2-draft: none, sha256-chain-prefix, sha256-chain-canonical, sha256-prev-raw, sha256-prev-field, sha256-canonical-fields; merkle-tlog added in 1.4.3-draft (EXT-026) from this capture. The verifier_key below is log.vkey as the capture wrote it.

integrity.documentation: RFC 6962 section 2.1 Merkle Tree Hash (leaf = SHA-256(0x00 || entry), node = SHA-256(0x01 || left || right)); C2SP tlog-tiles, tlog-checkpoint and signed-note; recomputable with the Python standard library (conformance.py merkle-tlog, examples/third-party/tessera-live/verify_tlog.py)
integrity.note: Up to 1.4.2-draft this adapter declared `none`, because the checker could not recompute a Merkle tree and declaring a hash-chain mechanism would have been a fake pass. merkle-tlog (1.4.3-draft, EXT-026) recomputes the tree from the entries' `data` (UTF-8 bytes as Tessera stored them), requires each `index` to equal its leaf position, requires the checkpoint's size and root to equal the tree's and the ones in its note, and verifies the note's Ed25519 signature under the verifier key above. The key is the one the capture job generated; the same job held the signing key (see independence), so the signature establishes that the checkpoint is the one that job signed, not that anyone else vouched for it. A rewrite by the key holder is detectable only against a checkpoint held by someone else (--expect-head; --expect-root for an earlier size): here checkpoint.round1, root d1d2ed1574b70efc82f33f01678111d11e0887d180463251eb52f387a9836519 (hex) over the first three entries. Signature verification is the checker's own RFC 8032 code; inclusion and consistency proofs are not read by the checker (it recomputes the whole tree instead); verify_tlog.py checks those.

loss.note: The signed checkpoint states the tree size, and entry indices are contiguous from 0 (Tessera README, Sequencing: 'All index numbers are contiguous and start from 0'), so a delivered set that is short of the signed size is detectable. Up to 1.4.2-draft only verify_tlog.py detected it: the checker could not tell the size was signed and failed VLC-L2-1. From 1.4.3-draft merkle-tlog recomputes the size and root the checkpoint states, so the produced count is read from a bound record and the checker detects it too. What the log cannot account for is an entry that never got an index: the same README section says an entry held in memory before sequencing is lost if the process dies, and the log records nothing of it.

coverage.note: The log records what was submitted to it. It does not state what should have been submitted: the capture chose which six statements to append, and a statement never submitted leaves no trace.

policy.note: The entries are opaque bytes to the log. The capture wrote a decision and a rule name into each statement, but the log binds no policy: it would have accepted any bytes, and nothing ties a statement's decision to a rule set.

independence.boundary_statement: In this capture the same runner job wrote the statements, held the signing key and could rewrite the log directory, so the log is independent of nothing it records. A transparency log's protection against its own operator comes from other parties holding checkpoints -- witnesses cosigning them, monitors checking consistency; Tessera supports a witness policy (posix-oneshot --witness_policy_file) and none was configured here. A Rekor v2 deployment separates submitters from the operator; that was not captured.
